also: what is there to see here?

terms.gloss: go and see (a city, its sights)
terms.grammar: with the accusative of the place or the thing seen: urbem vīsere
evidence: Liv. 23.7: vīsendā urbe magnam partem diēī cōnsūmpsit
Cic. Verr. 2.4.5: Messānam ut quisque nostrum vēnerat, haec vīsere solēbat
terms.comment: The word for going to look at a place for its own sake: Hannibal spends most of a day seeing Capua, and every Roman who came to Messana went to see the statues in one man’s house. Under “visit” the same verb is for calling on a person.

terms.gloss: the sights, what there is to see
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.132: ad ea quae vīsenda sunt
Cic. Verr. 2.4.135: quae apud quōsque vīsenda sunt
terms.comment: Cicero’s way of saying “the sights”: a relative clause with the gerundive, not a noun.

terms.gloss: for sightseeing, to see the place

phrases.latin: Hodiē urbem vīsēmus: castellum, forum, portum.
phrases.english: Today we’ll see the sights: the castle, the square, the harbour.
What is there to see here?

phrases.latin: vīsendā urbe magnam partem diēī cōnsūmpsit
phrases.english: he spent a large part of the day seeing the city

phrases.latin: iī quī hospitēs ad ea quae vīsenda sunt solent dūcere et ūnum quidque ostendere
phrases.english: those who usually take visitors round the sights and show them each thing
